derivations.claim: Fix a Cartesian orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $\mathbb C^3$ and $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$. Since $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)$ has rank one, at least one of $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)e_1,P_\sigma(\mathbf n)e_2,P_\sigma(\mathbf n)e_3$ is nonzero. Define $j_\sigma(\mathbf n)$ to be the least such index. The matrix fields $P_\sigma$ are smooth, so each set $\{\mathbf n:j_\sigma(\mathbf n)=j\}$ is Borel: it is the intersection of $\{\|P_\sigma e_j\|>0\}$ with the finitely many preceding zero sets. On that set define $e_\sigma(\mathbf n)=P_\sigma(\mathbf n)e_j/\|P_\sigma(\mathbf n)e_j\|$. The denominator is positive on its defining Borel set, so the piecewise formula is Borel, has unit norm, and lies in the range of $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)$.

At each $\mathbf n$, the vectors $e_+(\mathbf n),e_-(\mathbf n)$ are orthonormal because the projectors are orthogonal, and they span $P(\mathbf n)\mathbb C^3$ because their ranges are the two rank-one summands of $P(\mathbf n)$. For every transverse representative $f(\mathbf k)$, the fiberwise expansion is $f(\mathbf k)=\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}e_\sigma(\mathbf n(\mathbf k))\bigl(\overline{e_\sigma(\mathbf n(\mathbf k))}\cdot f(\mathbf k)\bigr)$ and $|f(\mathbf k)|^2=\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}|(Tf)(\mathbf k,\sigma)|^2$. Borel measurability of $e_\sigma$ makes $Tf$ measurable, and integration gives $\|Tf\|_{L^2(X)}=\|f\|_{\mathcal H_T^\nu}$. Conversely, for any $g\in L^2(X)$ the field $f(\mathbf k)=\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}e_\sigma(\mathbf n(\mathbf k))g(\mathbf k,\sigma)$ is measurable, transverse and square-integrable, and $Tf=g$. Hence $T$ is unitary.

On each fiber $h e_\sigma=\sigma e_\sigma$ and $P_\tau e_\sigma=\mathbf1_{\{\tau=\sigma\}}e_\sigma$. Substituting the fiberwise expansion from step 2.1 gives $Thf(\mathbf k,\sigma)=\sigma Tf(\mathbf k,\sigma)$ and $TP_\tau f(\mathbf k,\sigma)=\mathbf1_{\{\tau=\sigma\}}Tf(\mathbf k,\sigma)$ for every transverse field class. These are precisely the two multiplication-operator identities in the Statement.

derivations.claim: Fix $\mathbf n\in S^2$ and $v\in P(\mathbf n)\mathbb C^3$, so $\mathbf n\cdot v=0$. Under [A1], the rotation supplier [F2] provides the stated total operator on the common domain. Decompose $e_i=n_i\mathbf n+(e_i-n_i\mathbf n)$. The cross product of the two vectors $e_i-n_i\mathbf n$ and $v$, both perpendicular to $\mathbf n$, is parallel to $\mathbf n$, so projection by $P$ removes it; hence $P(e_i\times v)=n_i(\mathbf n\times v)$. Since $S_i v=i(e_i\times v)$ by the stated Levi-Civita convention, $P S_i P v=i n_i(\mathbf n\times v)=n_i h(\mathbf n)v$. Therefore the two displayed multiplication formulas for $S_i'$ agree on every transverse fiber.

The multiplier $n_i h(\mathbf n)$ is self-adjoint on the transverse fiber because $n_i$ is real and $h^*=h$, and its norm is at most $1$ because $|n_i|\le1$ and $\|h\|=1$ there. Integrating the fiberwise Hermitian identity shows that $S_i'$ is symmetric on the whole Hilbert space; since it is bounded and defined everywhere, the adjoint definition gives $S_i'^*=S_i'$. Its norm is at most $\hbar$. Its matrix coefficients are smooth on $M$; multiplication therefore preserves smoothness and compact support away from $\mathbf k=0$, and its values remain transverse by [F1]. Consequently $S_i'\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal D$, and $L_i'=J_i-S_i'$ on $D(J_i)$ is well-defined and restricts to an operator from $\mathcal D$ to $\mathcal H_T^\nu$.

It suffices first to consider the axis $e_3$. The $z$-axis and the positive-$x$ branch cut, with the origin removed, are $
u$-null by [F8]: on each annulus $1/m\le|\mathbf k|\le m$, the mass-shell density is bounded and both sets lie in Lebesgue-null coordinate hyperplanes. To apply the Borel change-of-variables formula [F4] to an arbitrary $f\in\mathcal H_T^
u$, take a finite-valued representative and apply [F11] to the Lebesgue-measurable sublevel sets of each of its six real components at rational levels. Countable Choice lets us select the corresponding Borel sets; their symmetric differences lie in a countable union of Borel null sets. Outside that union, each component equals the infimum of the rational levels whose selected Borel sets contain $\mathbf k$; defining each infimum to be $0$ on the union gives Borel real-valued representatives, hence a Borel vector representative $f_0=f$ almost everywhere. Since $d
u=(2|\mathbf k|)^{-1}d\lambda_3$ has strictly positive finite density on $M$, Lebesgue-null and $
u$-null sets there coincide. Thus $f_0$ represents the same Hilbert-space class, and [F4] applies to its coordinate pullback; the same formula shows the pullback is independent of the representative. Use the cylindrical coordinates of [F4], put $r=\sqrt{ho^2+z^2}$ and $\mathbf n_0(ho,z)=(ho,0,z)/r$, and define $g(ho,z,\phi)=R_{e_3}(-\phi)f_0(ho\cos\phi,ho\sin\phi,z)$. The rotation matrices preserve the Hermitian norm, so the measure identity and its inverse coordinate map $f_0(\mathbf k)=R_{e_3}(\phi)g(ho,z,\phi)$ make this a unitary identification with the subspace of $L^2(\Omega	imes\mathbb T,w\,dho\,dz\,d\phi/(2\pi);\mathbb C^3)$ satisfying $\mathbf n_0(ho,z)\cdot g(ho,z,\phi)=0$. Direct substitution gives $U(R_{e_3}(t))g(ho,z,\phi)=g(ho,z,\phi-t)$.

Write $g_m(\rho,z)=\int_{\mathbb T}g(\rho,z,\phi)e^{-im\phi}\,d\phi/(2\pi)$. By [F5], Parseval identifies the squared norm with $\sum_m\|g_m\|_{L^2(\Omega,w)}^2$, and the rotation difference quotient has Fourier coefficients $(e^{-imt}-1)g_m/t$. If $\sum_m m^2\|g_m\|^2<\infty$, then $|(e^{-imt}-1)/t|\le|m|$ and dominated convergence in the square-summable coefficient space gives convergence to $(-im g_m)_m$. Conversely, if the difference quotients converge in norm, their $m$th coefficients converge to $-im g_m$; Fatou applied to finite partial sums and then their increasing limit gives $\sum_m m^2\|g_m\|^2<\infty$. By [F10], this is exactly $D(J_{e_3})$; the generator acts as $J_{e_3}=-i\hbar\partial_\phi$ in the rotating coordinates, and the squared graph norm is $\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}(1+\hbar^2m^2)\|g_m\|_{L^2(\Omega,w)}^2$.

Let $g$ represent any vector in $D(J_{e_3})$. For $n\ge2$ use the explicit cutoffs $\chi_n$ from [F7]. They lie in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, satisfy $0\le\chi_n\le1$, and converge pointwise to $1$. Since $\chi_n$ depends only on $(\rho,z)$, it commutes with the $\phi$-derivative. Dominated convergence [F9] therefore gives $\chi_ng\to g$ in the graph norm of [F3]. Its Fourier truncations $g^{(N)}=\sum_{|m|\le N}\chi_ng_m e^{im\phi}$ converge in that graph norm by the weighted Parseval sum in step 2.1.

Fix $n,N$ and put $\eta_n=\chi_{2n}$; [F7] makes $\eta_n=1$ on the support of $\chi_n$ and gives compact support inside $\Omega$. Each of the finitely many coefficients $\chi_ng_m$ is supported in $\operatorname{supp}\chi_n$ and lies in $\mathbf n_0^\perp$. Extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^2$. On the compact support of $\eta_n$, the weight in [F4] is bounded above and below by positive constants, so [F6] gives a smooth compactly supported approximation $a_m^0$ in the weighted norm. Replace it by $a_m=\eta_nP(\mathbf n_0)a_m^0$. Because $P(\mathbf n_0)\chi_ng_m=\chi_ng_m$ and $\|P\|\le1$, this is transverse and does not increase the approximation error. Choose the finitely many coefficient errors so that $\sum_{|m|\le N}(1+\hbar^2m^2)\|a_m-\chi_ng_m\|^2$ is arbitrarily small. Then $\sum_{|m|\le N}a_m(\rho,z)e^{im\phi}$ is smooth, transverse, and compactly supported away from $\rho=0$; after applying $R_{e_3}(\phi)$ and returning to $\mathbf k$ coordinates it is an element of $\mathcal D$, since both factors are $2\pi$-periodic and their derivatives match across the angular seam. Combining these finite coefficient approximations with the cutoff and Fourier truncation from step 3.1 gives graph convergence to $g$, so $\mathcal D$ is a core for $J_{e_3}$.

For any unit $\mathbf a$, choose $R\in SO(3)$ with $Re_3=\mathbf a$. The rotation representation gives $U(R)U(R_{e_3}(t))U(R)^*=U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))$; Stone uniqueness then gives $J_{\mathbf a}=U(R)J_{e_3}U(R)^*$ with the conjugated domain. Also $U(R)\mathcal D=\mathcal D$, because rotations preserve smoothness, compact support away from zero, and transversality. Applying the unitary $U(R)$ to the graph-dense approximation in step 4.1 proves that $\mathcal D$ is a core for $J_{\mathbf a}$.

derivations.claim: The domain $\mathcal D$ is invariant under each $J_i$ and $S_i'$ by their smooth differential and multiplication formulas. Write $X_i=(e_i\times\mathbf k)\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf k}$ and $C_i v=e_i\times v$, so $L_i=-i\hbar X_i$ and $\hbar S_i=i\hbar C_i$. The product rule for the linear vector fields gives $[X_i,X_j]f=(e_j\times(e_i\times\mathbf k)-e_i\times(e_j\times\mathbf k))\cdot\nabla f=-\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}X_k f$. The vector triple-product identity gives $[C_i,C_j]=\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}C_k$, while constant matrices commute with the scalar differential coefficients, so $[L_i,\hbar S_j]=0$. Therefore $[L_i,L_j]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$ and $[\hbar S_i,\hbar S_j]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}\hbar S_k$. Adding these identities yields $[J_i,J_j]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$ on $\mathcal D$.

Since $J_i$ is self-adjoint and $-S_i'$ is bounded self-adjoint, it is $J_i$-bounded with relative-bound coefficient $a=0<1$ and finite constant $b=\|S_i'\|$. Apply [F4] to $A=J_i$ and $B=-S_i'$ to conclude $L_i'=J_i-S_i'$ is self-adjoint on exactly $D(J_i)$. For every $\psi\in D(J_i)$, $\|L_i'\psi\|\le\|J_i\psi\|+\hbar\|\psi\|$ and $\|J_i\psi\|\le\|L_i'\psi\|+\hbar\|\psi\|$. These inequalities make the two graph norms equivalent. Hence [F3] implies that $\mathcal D$ is also a core for $L_i'$.

The operators $S_i'$ are multiplication by the commuting matrix fields $\hbar n_i h(\mathbf n)$. Thus on every transverse fiber $S_i'S_j'=\hbar^2 n_i n_j h^2=S_j'S_i'$, so $[S_i',S_j']=0$ as bounded operators, in particular on $\mathcal D$.

For $R\in SO(3)$, the cross-product identity $(R\mathbf n)\times(Rv)=R(\mathbf n\times v)$ gives $P(R\mathbf n)=RP(\mathbf n)R^{-1}$ and $h(R\mathbf n)=Rh(\mathbf n)R^{-1}$. Also $RS_jR^{-1}=\sum_m R_{mj}S_m$, since rotations carry $e_j$ to $\sum_mR_{mj}e_m$. Substituting these identities in $S_j'(\mathbf n)=\hbar P(\mathbf n)S_jP(\mathbf n)$ yields $U(R)S_j'U(R)^*=\sum_mR_{mj}S_m'$. For $R=R_{e_i}(t)$, differentiating the right side at zero gives $\sum_m\epsilon_{ijm}S_m'$. For $\psi\in\mathcal D$, both $\psi$ and $S_j'\psi$ lie in $D(J_i)$ by [F1]–[F2], so the product rule for the left side gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}U(R_{e_i}(t))S_j'U(R_{e_i}(t))^*\psi=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[J_i,S_j']\psi$. Equating the two derivatives proves $[J_i,S_j']=i\hbar\sum_m\epsilon_{ijm}S_m'$ on $\mathcal D$.

Using $L_i'=J_i-S_i'$ and invariance of $\mathcal D$, expand on $\mathcal D$: $[L_i',S_j']=[J_i,S_j']-[S_i',S_j']=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}S_k'$, and $[L_i',L_j']=[J_i,J_j]-[J_i,S_j']-[S_i',J_j]+[S_i',S_j']=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}(J_k-2S_k')=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}(L_k'-S_k')$. Here $[S_i',J_j]=-[J_j,S_i']=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}S_k'$ because $\epsilon_{jik}=-\epsilon_{ijk}$. Along with step 1.3 and step 1.1, these are all stated identities. The term $-S_k'$ in the orbital commutator prevents $L_i'$ from satisfying an independent $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ algebra; the commuting $S_i'$ also do not satisfy the nonzero $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ brackets.

derivations.claim: For $R\in SO(3)$, $U(R)^{\otimes n}$ commutes with the permutation action on $\mathcal H_T^{\widehat\otimes n}$, so it preserves the symmetric sector and is unitary there; set its vacuum-sector value to $1$. The tensor and direct-sum definitions in [F2] give $\Gamma(U(R_1))\Gamma(U(R_2))=\Gamma(U(R_1R_2))$. On an elementary tensor, the telescoping estimate $\|\bigotimes_rU(R)\psi_r-\bigotimes_rU(R_0)\psi_r\|\le\sum_j\|U(R)\psi_j-U(R_0)\psi_j\|\prod_{r\ne j}\|\psi_r\|$ shows strong continuity from that of $U$. Density extends it to each symmetric sector; finite-particle vectors are dense by [F2], and approximation by such vectors with unitarity extends continuity to the full Fock direct sum. For each axis, Stone's theorem [F7] supplies the unique self-adjoint generator $J_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm F}$. For $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_n\in D(J_{\mathbf a})$, differentiating the finite tensor product at $t=0$ by the product rule gives the sum of the one-particle derivatives $-iJ_{\mathbf a}\psi_r/\hbar$; symmetrization commutes with the tensor action. Hence the Stone generator acts on these finite symmetric tensors by the displayed $d\Gamma(J_{\mathbf a})$ sum.

Apply the unitary $T$ of [F4] and its Fock lift $\Gamma(T)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T^{\otimes_s n}$. Each sector map is unitary because tensor powers preserve inner products and commute with permutations, so $\Gamma(T)$ is unitary. Put $X=M\times\{+1,-1\}$ and $\boldsymbol\omega(\mathbf k,\sigma)=(|\mathbf k|,\mathbf1_{\{\sigma=+1\}},\mathbf1_{\{\sigma=-1\}})$. The measure $\nu\otimes\#$ is sigma-finite by the bundle definition in [F3], and $\boldsymbol\omega$ is finite-valued and measurable. The three coordinates in [F5] therefore give the self-adjoint Fock multipliers $H_0=d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$, $N_+$, and $N_-$ on their exact domains; the third linear combination $H_{(0,1,-1)}$ is the self-adjoint sector multiplier $\sum_r\sigma_r=d\Gamma(h)$. On each finite-particle sector, $\mathbf1_{\{\sigma=+1\}}-\mathbf1_{\{\sigma=-1\}}=\sigma$, so this operator agrees there with the difference $N_+-N_-$. Its full domain is the exact $D(H_{(0,1,-1)})$ supplied by [F5], not an informal difference of unbounded operators.

The space $\mathscr D_{\rm fin}(\mathcal D)$ is dense because $\mathcal D$ is dense in $\mathcal H_T^\nu$ by [F3], algebraic tensors are dense in each Hilbert tensor completion, and finite-particle truncations are dense in the direct sum by [F2]. It is invariant under the sector sums $d\Gamma(J_i)$ because $J_i\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal D$ by [F3]. On an elementary $n$-tensor, expanding each sector sum shows that terms acting on distinct tensor factors commute, while terms on the same factor give $[J_i,J_j]$; hence $[d\Gamma(J_i),d\Gamma(J_j)]=\sum_{r=1}^n[J_i,J_j]^{(r)}=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}d\Gamma(J_k)$ on the symmetrized tensor core by [F6]. This is the asserted Fock total rotation algebra.

In the scalarized one-particle representation, $V_t$ is multiplication by $e^{-it|\mathbf k|}$ on both helicity components, so its Fock lift is the phase group $e^{-itH_0}$ from [F5]. The joint spectral measure in [F5] makes this group commute with every Borel function of the helicity coordinates, in particular with $H_{(0,1,-1)}=d\Gamma(h)$; the joint multiplier also preserves its exact domain. Thus $\Gamma(V_t)D_h=D_h\Gamma(V_t)$ for every real $t$, proving the conservation statement.

If $P_\sigma f=f$, then $hf=\sigma f$ by [F4]. By [F6], $S_z'f(\mathbf k)=\hbar n_z(\mathbf k)h(\mathbf n(\mathbf k))f(\mathbf k)=\hbar\sigma\cos\theta(\mathbf k)f(\mathbf k)$. Taking the Hilbert pairing with $f$, using $\|f\|_\nu=1$ and $n_z=k_z/|\mathbf k|=\cos\theta$, gives the displayed expectation identity. The multiplier is bounded, so the integral is finite.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
